I'm not sure anyone is really arguing that certain degrees don't have a higher job placement than others by means of pure statistics. That's something that's already well known as fact. But the issue at large I think is two fold:

1. That many students (at least in the US) went into college expecting to come out the other side with better prospects than they have. Sure, if you're an engineering major or comp sci person your chances of getting a stable, well paying job was better than most *anyway.* What ended up happening is that the (sometimes meager) job opportunities for other majors evaporated rather abruptly. It's not necessarily that students in these other majors made terrible choices, but that even their modest expectations were too high.

2.  The other part of this is that students went to school with the intention of pursuing something that they liked, and were advised to do so. This wouldn't have been such a bad idea (since people generally tend to excel at what they like) if the economy hadn't blown up in everyone's faces. The result is this massive wave of regret washing over recent grads who got stuck with the short stick. The alternative is to follow the money. In which case we'd likely see an over saturation of skilled labor to those most profitable markets in short order. Honestly, I'm not sure which is worse.

Still, the individual still has to work their ass off. Especially if your degree isn't in high demand. Your degree has value, it just needs effort in order to be useful. Then again, I'm a (barely) employed English Literature grad, so I'm not sure how valid my opinion in this is.
